Please review the following manuscript written by my collaborator.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b06/review-experiment-nk_e5y4z/call-b8a39e1592b345ea801551fa5d443c38/manuscript.pdf

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c 'ls -l manuscript.pdf; command -v pdftotext; command -v pdftoppm; command -v pdfinfo; command -v python3'

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
out=Path('tmp/pdfs')
out.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
print('PAGES',len(r.pages))
print('METADATA',r.metadata)
texts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
    text=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
    (out/f'page-{i:02}.txt').write_text(text)
    texts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n'+text)
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts)[:43000])
PY"

strengths: Addresses a relevant provenance problem with a modular approach compatible with existing bitstring watermarking systems.
Theorems 1 and 4 provide interpretable conditional bounds connecting decoding accuracy and codeword separation to detection and attribution performance. Algorithm pseudocode is provided.

Image experiments cover three generation models, populations up to one million users, and both average and worst-user performance. Figure 7 provides evidence that A-BSTA improves attribution for poorly performing users compared with Random and NRG under JPEG compression.
weaknesses: Theorem 3 contains a substantive probability error: Appendix A.4 factors match-event probabilities even though they share the same decoded watermark. For n=2, threshold 0.9 and uniform decoded bits, independently sampling w1 from {00,01} and w2 from {10,11} gives FDR=1/2, exceeding the claimed bound of 7/16. Furthermore, Section 7.6 applies this theorem to A-BSTA's dependently constructed codebooks. The false-detection guarantees require revision.

The binomial analysis assumes independent decoded bits and identical per-bit accuracy for each user, without validating these assumptions, particularly after post-processing. The described aggregate bias estimate also does not establish the coordinatewise condition required for gamma. Agreement between average empirical rates and bounds fitted using the same test data does not validate rare-error guarantees. Likewise, similar lower bounds alone do not establish the claim in Section 6.5 that detection implies correct attribution.

Novelty and baseline coverage are insufficient. Assigning user codewords and applying nearest-Hamming decoding closely connects to established digital fingerprinting and error-correcting codes, but this literature is inadequately addressed. A-BSTA mainly adds depth truncation and random initialization to an existing algorithm. Comparisons against standard coded-ID constructions, such as BCH codebooks, are missing. Table 1 also shows that random initialization benefits NRG, making controlled initialization and matched-runtime comparisons necessary.

The evidence does not substantiate reliable attribution at the claimed deployment scale. FDR is evaluated on only 1,000 non-AI images; even zero observed errors yields an approximately 0.3% one-sided 95% upper confidence bound. The 100-million-user result assumes decoding accuracy and codebook geometry rather than evaluating a constructed system, and Table 4 reports an FDR upper bound of 6%. End-to-end attribution latency and codebook construction costs at that scale are unreported.

Robustness conclusions exceed the tested conditions. Common transformations largely overlap with training, while black-box evaluation uses one attack that reduces TDR and TAR to zero at every reported budget, albeit with substantial image degradation. This establishes a quality cost for that particular attack. Broader claims require unseen and composed transformations, regeneration attacks, and attribution-specific collusion or framing evaluations.

Content quality and cross-modal applicability are insufficiently demonstrated. Images are evaluated at 128×128, and reported SSIM compares watermarked images with post-processed versions, leaving the original-to-watermarked quality cost unmeasured. The text study uses human-authored WikiText-2 segments and one constrained paraphraser, with no fluency or semantic-preservation evaluation despite a large watermark-loss weight. This provides limited evidence for practical attribution of AI-generated text.
